title: A Vesicle Can Carry A Signal

scenes.visual: Title card: A Vesicle Can Carry A Signal.

scenes.tts: Cells release tiny sacs of membrane called extracellular vesicles. These vesicles can carry a signal from one cell to another. The clearest case comes from the immune system. B cells release vesicles that carry M H C class two molecules, each holding a peptide. Those vesicles switch on T cells, but only the T cells whose receptor recognises that peptide. Nothing has to get inside. A scrap of membrane can show a T cell what a whole B cell would show it.
scenes.visual: A B cell on the left releases small teal vesicles studded with MHC molecules, each holding an orange peptide. They drift to two T cells on the right. One T cell's receptor matches the peptide and lights up gold; the other, with a different receptor, stays grey. A label reads: nothing enters the cell.
scenes.narration: Cells release tiny sacs of membrane called extracellular vesicles. These vesicles can carry a signal from one cell to another. The clearest case comes from the immune system. B cells release vesicles that carry MHC class II molecules, each holding a peptide. Those vesicles switch on T cells, but only the T cells whose receptor recognises that peptide. Nothing has to get inside. A scrap of membrane can show a T cell what a whole B cell would show it.

scenes.tts: Where do these vesicles come from? The answer starts inside the cell. The membrane of a compartment called an endosome buds inward, away from the cytosol, the cell's own fluid. It pinches off small vesicles into its own interior, and these carry receptors. A compartment packed with them is a multivesicular body. In B cells, compartments like this are where M H C class two is loaded with peptide.
scenes.visual: Zoom into the B cell. A large round compartment sits in the yellow-tinted cytosol. Its membrane pushes inward, away from that fluid, and pinches off vesicles filled with it, one after another; MHC molecules appear on them and the compartment is named multivesicular body.

scenes.tts: Picture this compartment as a sorting room with two doors, one to the incinerator and one to the street. If it fuses with a lysosome, its vesicles and their cargo are digested. If it moves to the cell surface and fuses with the plasma membrane, its vesicles are released intact. Those released vesicles are exosomes. The route was first seen in young red blood cells, throwing out transferrin receptors they no longer needed.
scenes.visual: Reuse the two-door animation: door one, the compartment slides into a lysosome and its vesicles turn red and vanish; door two, a fresh compartment rises to the surface, opens into the membrane and the vesicles float out intact, named exosomes. A small inset shows a red blood cell releasing vesicles carrying blue receptors.

scenes.tts: The direction of budding fixes the geometry. The bud forms away from the cytosol, so the inside of an exosome is a sample of cytosol, and its outer face is the face that was the outside of the cell. So a receptor, or an M H C molecule, still points outward, as it did on the plasma membrane. That is why a vesicle can show a ligand to another cell.
scenes.visual: Reuse the budding-geometry animation, with MHC molecules in place of the receptors: a bud grows into the compartment, open to the cytosol, and pinches off as a cytosol-filled vesicle with its MHC molecules pointing out. The plasma membrane on the right shows its MHC pointing out too; gold arrows mark both.

scenes.tts: A vesicle could act on another cell in three ways. A ligand on its surface can bind a receptor on the target, and nothing has to get in. The vesicle can fuse with a membrane of the target and release its contents into the cytosol. Or the target can swallow it. Swallowing alone shows little, because what a cell swallows usually ends in the lysosome.
scenes.visual: Three panels, matching the lesson figure: a vesicle ligand binding a receptor on the target surface (gold signal arrow); a vesicle fusing and spilling its contents into the cytosol; a vesicle swallowed into an endosome that heads to a lysosome, with a question mark.

scenes.tts: Proving a case takes controls, because the centrifuge that collects vesicles also brings down protein clumps and other particles of the same size. Ask whether the activity floats with the vesicles on a density gradient, and whether it is specific, as the T cell response was. And mind the name. Vesicles that bud straight from the cell surface look the same, so unless you can show where a vesicle formed, call it an extracellular vesicle.
scenes.visual: A centrifuge tube whose pellet holds vesicles mixed with grey protein clumps. The pellet is floated on a gradient: vesicles rise to a band and the activity marker rises with them, while the clumps stay below. Then an exosome and a microvesicle, budded from the surface, side by side and identical; one label covers both: extracellular vesicle.
